### Problem 1
#### Dataset Description
```{r load-noaa}
data("ny_noaa")

dim(ny_noaa)
names(ny_noaa)
summary(ny_noaa)
```
The `ny_noaa` dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables from `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` weather stations in New York State. The observations span from `r min(ny_noaa$date)` to `r max(ny_noaa$date)`. Key variables include station ID (`id`), date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

Missing data are present in several variables, including `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa$prcp))` missing values for precipitation, `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa$snow))` for snowfall, `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa$snwd))` for snow depth, `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa$tmax))` for maximum temperature, and `r sum(is.na(ny_noaa$tmin))` for minimum temperature. In addition, `tmax` and `tmin` are currently stored as character variables and will need to be converted during data cleaning.

#### Data Cleaning and Snowfall
```{r clean-noaa}
ny_noaa =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date),
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    snow = snow,
    snwd = snwd,
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  )
```

```{r snowfall-frequency}
ny_noaa |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)
```

The most commonly observed snowfall value is `r ny_noaa |> filter(!is.na(snow)) |> count(snow, sort = TRUE) |> slice(1) |> pull(snow)` mm. Other common snowfall values include `r ny_noaa |> filter(!is.na(snow)) |> count(snow, sort = TRUE) |> slice(2:5) |> pull(snow) |> paste(collapse = ", ")` mm. The large number of 0 mm observations is expected because snowfall does not occur on most station-days. The repeated nonzero values likely reflect commonly reported snowfall amounts and rounding in the measurement process.

#### Average Maximum Temperature in January and July

```{r}
temp_month_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(!is.nan(mean_tmax)) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )
```

```{r}
temp_month_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  )
```

January temperatures are much lower and more variable than July temperatures. The mean January maximum temperature is `r temp_month_df |> filter(month == "January") |> summarize(mean(mean_tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull() |> round(1)` °C, compared with `r temp_month_df |> filter(month == "July") |> summarize(mean(mean_tmax, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull() |> round(1)` °C in July. Both months show clear year-to-year variation across stations, but July temperatures are more tightly clustered. A few unusually low station-year averages appear to be potential outliers, especially in January.

#### Temperature and Snowfall Distributions

```{r}
temp_snow_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin))

temp_snow_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, size = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum temperature (C)",
    y = "Maximum temperature (C)"
  )
```

```{r}
ny_noaa |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Snowfall by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1)
  )
```

Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship, with a correlation of `r cor(ny_noaa$tmin, ny_noaa$tmax, use = "complete.obs") |> round(2)`. A few extreme temperature observations are visible outside the main cluster. For snowfall values between 0 and 100 mm, the yearly distributions are generally similar, with an overall median of `r ny_noaa |> filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |> summarize(median(snow, na.rm = TRUE)) |> pull()` mm and only modest variation across years.


### Problem 2
#### Data Cleaning
```{r}
nhanes_covar =
  read_csv(
    "data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4
  )

nhanes_accel =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")

head(nhanes_covar)
names(nhanes_accel)[1:6]
tail(names(nhanes_accel))
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_clean =
  nhanes_covar |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )

nhanes_accel_long =
  nhanes_accel |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "MIMS"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = parse_number(minute)
  )

nhanes_df =
  nhanes_covar_clean |>
  inner_join(nhanes_accel_long, by = "SEQN")
```

```{r}
glimpse(nhanes_df)
n_distinct(nhanes_df$SEQN)
```
After cleaning and merging the demographic and accelerometer data, the final dataset contains `r n_distinct(nhanes_df$SEQN)` participants and `r nrow(nhanes_df)` minute-level observations. Participants younger than 21 years and those with missing demographic data were excluded, and sex and education were encoded as factors.

#### Demographic Table and Age Distribution
```{r}
demographic_table =
  nhanes_covar_clean |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  )

knitr::kable(
  demographic_table,
  caption = "Number of Participants by Education Level and Sex"
)
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex"
  )
```
The largest education group is "More than high school," with `r sum(nhanes_covar_clean$education == "More than high school")` participants and similar numbers of men and women. The "High school equivalent" group has more men than women, while the "Less than high school" group is nearly balanced by sex. The age distributions overlap substantially within each education category, although some differences in shape are visible between men and women, particularly in the higher education groups.

#### Total Daily Activity
```{r}
total_activity_df =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(SEQN, sex, age, BMI, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_activity = sum(MIMS, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r}
total_activity_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age",
    y = "Total daily activity",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Total daily activity generally decreases with age across all three education groups. The smoothed trends suggest some differences between men and women, although these patterns vary by education level. Overall, activity levels tend to be lower at older ages.
